items.stem: A 33-year-old G1P0 at 11 weeks has a cell-free DNA screen reported as no result because the fetal fraction was 2 percent. Her body mass index is 41. What is the best next step?
options: Reassure her that the test is negative and recommend routine care
Offer counseling and further testing, since low fetal fraction raises aneuploidy risk
Repeat the same test weekly until a result is reported
Schedule amniocentesis next week without discussing options
items.explanation: A failed cell-free DNA result from low fetal fraction is not a negative screen, and it is associated with a higher chance of aneuploidy, notably trisomy 18 and 13, along with higher body mass index. Counseling should offer detailed ultrasonography and diagnostic testing or alternative screening. Treating it as negative is wrong, and repeated redraws often fail again while an invasive test is a choice, not an automatic requirement.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman undergoing in vitro fertilization has had an egg retrieval 6 days ago and now has abdominal distension, nausea, and dyspnea. Ultrasound shows ascites and enlarged ovaries and her hematocrit is 50 percent. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate bilateral oophorectomy
Outpatient diuretics to reduce the ascites
Repeat gonadotropin stimulation next cycle
Admission for fluid support and thromboprophylaxis
items.explanation: Severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome produces third spacing, hemoconcentration, and thrombosis risk, so supportive admission with careful fluids, paracentesis when needed, and thromboprophylaxis is appropriate. Oophorectomy is not required. Diuretics further contract intravascular volume and raise clot risk, and restarting stimulation is inappropriate while the syndrome is active. Severe cases can also require drainage of tense ascites to relieve dyspnea.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a 28-day cycle has a serum progesterone drawn on cycle day 21 to confirm ovulation. Which result best supports that ovulation occurred this cycle?
options: A value below 1 ng/mL with a high estradiol
A value that is identical to the day 7 sample
A value above 3 ng/mL
A value that rises only after menses begin
items.explanation: Progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum, so a mid-luteal level above 3 ng/mL indicates that ovulation took place. A low value with high estradiol suggests the follicular pattern without a corpus luteum. A level unchanged from the early follicular sample shows no luteal activity, and a rise after menses cannot reflect the luteal phase, which ends with menstruation.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman complains of fatigue, cold intolerance, and weight gain. Laboratory studies show TSH 12 mIU/L with a low free thyroxine, and a negative pregnancy test. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Levothyroxine
Liothyronine alone at a high dose
Propylthiouracil twice daily
Iodine supplementation alone
items.explanation: Overt hypothyroidism with a high TSH and low free thyroxine is treated with levothyroxine, with the dose adjusted until TSH is in the reference range. Liothyronine alone has a short half-life and fluctuating levels. Propylthiouracil treats hyperthyroidism and would worsen the condition, and iodine is useful only in the rare setting of deficiency, which is not the likely cause here.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman undergoes a pelvic lymphadenectomy as part of surgical staging for endometrial cancer. After surgery she has weakness of thigh adduction and numbness over the medial thigh. Which nerve was most likely injured?
options: Genitofemoral nerve
Femoral nerve
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
Obturator nerve
items.explanation: The obturator nerve runs along the pelvic sidewall through the obturator fossa, where it is exposed during pelvic lymph node dissection. Injury causes weak thigh adduction and medial thigh sensory loss. The genitofemoral nerve causes anterior upper thigh and labial sensory change, the femoral nerve causes weak knee extension, and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve causes lateral thigh numbness.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G3P2 at 27 weeks with anti-Kell antibodies has a titer of 1:32. The father is heterozygous for the Kell antigen. Which test is the best noninvasive way to assess for fetal anemia?
options: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity
Umbilical artery systolic to diastolic ratio
Amniotic fluid optical density at 450 nm by amniocentesis
Biophysical profile score
items.explanation: Middle cerebral artery Doppler peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median predicts moderate to severe fetal anemia and has replaced invasive amniotic fluid spectrophotometry. Umbilical artery Doppler evaluates placental resistance, not anemia. A biophysical profile can be normal until the fetus is severely compromised, so it is not a reliable screen for anemia, and the amniotic method is invasive.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has azoospermia on two semen analyses. He has small testes, a normal semen volume, and an elevated FSH of 28 mIU/mL. What is the most likely cause?
options: Obstruction of the vas deferens
Primary testicular failure
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
Retrograde ejaculation
items.explanation: A raised FSH with small testes and azoospermia points to impaired spermatogenesis within the testis, as in primary testicular failure, because the pituitary responds to low inhibin. Obstruction gives normal testicular size and normal FSH. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism causes low FSH, and retrograde ejaculation reduces volume and leaves sperm in the post-ejaculate urine. Karyotype and Y chromosome microdeletion testing are the usual next studies.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman of Ashkenazi Jewish descent tests negative on carrier screening for Tay-Sachs disease using a targeted mutation panel. Her partner is a known carrier. How should her result be interpreted?
options: Her risk is zero because the panel was negative
Her risk now equals the carrier frequency of the general population
Reduced but not eliminated, because of residual risk
Her risk is unchanged from before testing
items.explanation: Targeted panels detect only common variants, so a negative result lowers the probability of being a carrier without removing it. This residual risk is calculated from the panel detection rate and the prior carrier frequency. Calling the risk zero overstates what the test can do, and leaving the risk unchanged ignores the information gained from a negative panel result.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman with no prior fractures and no risk factors has never had bone density testing. She asks when screening should occur. Which is the best response?
options: Bone density testing now
Wait until she sustains a fracture before testing
Order an ultrasound of the heel every year
Begin testing at age 75
items.explanation: Screening with dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry is recommended for all women at 65, and earlier for younger postmenopausal women with higher fracture risk. Waiting for a fracture defeats prevention. Heel ultrasound is a less accurate substitute that does not guide treatment, and delaying until 75 would miss a decade in which treatment could reduce fractures. Results then guide therapy and follow-up intervals.

items.stem: During operative hysteroscopy using a glycine distending medium, the fluid deficit reaches 2,500 mL. The patient becomes confused and nauseated, and sodium is 118 mEq/L. What is the best initial management?
options: Continue to completion and monitor sodium afterward
Give large-volume hypotonic fluids to flush the excess
Stop, give a diuretic, and correct sodium slowly
Infuse 3 percent saline at the fastest rate possible
items.explanation: Absorption of hypotonic nonelectrolyte medium causes dilutional hyponatremia with cerebral edema, so the procedure is stopped, a diuretic is given, and sodium is corrected cautiously. Continuing risks seizure and death. Hypotonic fluids worsen the problem, and overly rapid correction with hypertonic saline can cause osmotic demyelination. Early recognition of a large fluid deficit allows the team to stop before symptoms develop, and careful monitoring of inflow and outflow is the best prevention.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G2P1 at 20 weeks had a prior newborn with intracranial hemorrhage from confirmed alloimmune thrombocytopenia. Her own platelet count is normal. Which maternal therapy is preferred in this pregnancy?
options: Weekly platelet transfusions given to the mother
Rh immune globulin once at 28 weeks
Intrauterine platelet transfusion with no maternal therapy
Weekly intravenous immune globulin with or without prednisone
items.explanation: Alloimmune thrombocytopenia arises when maternal antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal platelets, so the mother is treated with weekly intravenous immune globulin, sometimes with steroids, to reduce transplacental antibody. Transfusing the mother does not help the fetus. Rh immune globulin addresses red cell alloimmunization only, and intrauterine platelet transfusion is invasive with a high complication rate, reserved for refractory cases.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman who smokes no tobacco requests combined oral contraceptives. She has migraine with visual aura about twice a month. Her blood pressure is normal. Which is the best recommendation?
options: Prescribe a low-dose combined pill plus daily aspirin
Avoid estrogen and offer a progestin-only or copper method
Prescribe a vaginal ring for lower systemic exposure
Prescribe a transdermal patch with no restrictions
items.explanation: Migraine with aura raises the risk of ischemic stroke, and estrogen adds to that risk, so combined hormonal methods are category 4 and should not be used. Progestin-only methods and the copper intrauterine device are safe. Aspirin does not neutralize the added risk, and the ring and patch still deliver estrogen systemically. Such methods keep contraception effective without raising stroke risk.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman requests postpartum tubal ligation. She is on Medicaid and signed the federal sterilization consent form 20 days before her expected delivery. She delivers at 37 weeks. What is the correct approach?
options: Postpone it, since the 30-day waiting period was not met
Proceed, because delivery at 37 weeks waives the waiting period
Proceed once she signs a new form on the first postpartum day
Proceed once her husband also signs the consent form
items.explanation: Federally funded sterilization requires consent signed at least 30 days, and not more than 180 days, before the procedure, with an exception for premature delivery or emergency abdominal surgery when at least 72 hours have passed. Here the interval is 20 days and delivery at 37 weeks is not premature, so the procedure waits. Spousal consent is never required, and a new signature after delivery restarts the clock.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a mother who developed breast cancer at 42 and an aunt with ovarian cancer at 55. She asks whether genetic testing is appropriate. What is the best next step?
options: Begin annual mammography at age 25 only
Refer for genetic counseling and panel testing
Offer prophylactic mastectomy right away
Reassure her that family history does not matter
items.explanation: Early-onset breast cancer plus ovarian cancer in close relatives meets criteria for genetic risk assessment, and counseling ahead of multigene testing allows informed interpretation. Imaging alone without assessing risk may be the wrong schedule. Surgery before any testing is premature, and dismissing the history ignores a strong pattern suggestive of a hereditary syndrome. Test results then direct risk-reducing options.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has a painful 4 cm left Bartholin gland abscess with surrounding cellulitis. She is afebrile and otherwise healthy. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Needle aspiration followed by antibiotics alone
Complete excision of the gland under general anesthesia
Warm soaks and observation without drainage
Incision and drainage with placement of a Word catheter
items.explanation: A symptomatic Bartholin abscess is best drained, and a Word catheter left for several weeks keeps the tract open and forms an epithelialized duct that reduces recurrence. Aspiration alone often recurs, and antibiotics do not drain pus. Excision is reserved for recurrent cases and carries more morbidity, and soaks may help mild cysts but will not clear a large abscess.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 20 weeks is diagnosed with a proximal deep venous thrombosis and starts therapeutic anticoagulation. For how long should anticoagulation continue?
options: Until 34 weeks, then stop for delivery
For 4 weeks only, if her leg symptoms resolve
Through at least 6 weeks postpartum, for a minimum of 3 months in total
Until the day of delivery only
items.explanation: Pregnancy and the early puerperium are hypercoagulable, so treatment of venous thromboembolism is continued for the rest of the pregnancy and at least 6 weeks after birth, with at least 3 months of therapy in total. Stopping early or around delivery leaves her at risk of recurrence or pulmonary embolism, and symptom resolution does not mean the clot is treated. Therapy is interrupted only around labor, then resumed.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman took levonorgestrel emergency contraception 12 hours after unprotected intercourse. She asks whether the pill could end a pregnancy that has already implanted. Which response is most accurate?
options: It acts by dislodging an implanted embryo
It works mainly by delaying ovulation and does not disrupt an established pregnancy
It causes the uterine lining to shed at once
It is a form of medical abortion
items.explanation: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception acts mainly by delaying or inhibiting ovulation, so sperm and egg do not meet. It has no effect on an implanted pregnancy and it is not abortifacient in any way. It does not cause immediate endometrial shedding, and it differs fundamentally from mifepristone-based medical abortion, which blocks progesterone action in an established pregnancy, as mentioned.

items.stem: A rural hospital with 600 deliveries a year plans to manage a woman with a previously diagnosed placenta accreta spectrum and a planned cesarean hysterectomy. Which action best reflects the levels of maternal care?
options: Operate locally with a visiting general surgeon on call
Schedule a vaginal delivery to avoid surgical bleeding
Transfer her to a level III or IV maternal care center
Arrange blood on standby and proceed at the current site
items.explanation: Placenta accreta spectrum carries a high risk of massive hemorrhage and is best managed at a center with a multidisciplinary team, interventional radiology, and large-volume transfusion capacity, which defines level III or IV maternal care. Planned local surgery without that depth of resources is unsafe. Attempting vaginal delivery with an invasive placenta risks catastrophic bleeding, and blood on standby alone does not substitute for specialized expertise.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman reports two falls in the past year. She takes a sedative at night for sleep and walks slowly with a cane. What is the most useful initial intervention to reduce her fall risk?
options: Prescribe a stronger sleep medication
Advise strict bed rest at home
Recommend high-dose vitamin E daily
Stop the sedative and start balance and strength training
items.explanation: Falls are best reduced with a multifactorial approach, and sedative-hypnotics are among the most modifiable risks, so they are deprescribed while balance and strength exercise is begun. A stronger sedative would increase risk. Bed rest causes deconditioning and more falls, and vitamin E has no demonstrated benefit for fall prevention. Vision and home hazards should also be reviewed.

items.stem: During laparoscopic surgery with monopolar electrosurgery, a surgeon notes a burn on the bowel serosa away from the instrument tip, found at the site where the shaft was in contact with another loop. Which mechanism best explains this injury?
options: Capacitive coupling through intact insulation
Thermal spread from a bipolar vessel sealing instrument
Return electrode pad burn at the thigh
Cold light source heat at the trocar
items.explanation: Capacitive coupling occurs when current passes through intact insulation into a nearby conductor, such as bowel, and can injure tissue outside the surgeon's view. Bipolar thermal spread acts at the jaws of the instrument, and a return pad burn appears at the pad site on the skin. Fiberoptic light cables can ignite drapes but do not produce a remote serosal burn.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a spontaneous vaginal birth at term. Her syphilis infection was diagnosed at 38 weeks and she received one dose of benzathine penicillin G 10 days before delivery. The newborn is asymptomatic with a normal examination. What is the best approach for the newborn?
options: Reassure and discharge, since the mother received penicillin
Repeat the maternal titer and treat the newborn only if it rises
Evaluate for congenital syphilis, because treatment within 30 days of birth is inadequate
Give no testing because the newborn has no signs
items.explanation: Maternal syphilis therapy given less than 30 days before delivery is considered inadequate to protect the fetus, so the newborn is managed as having possible congenital syphilis. This means serologic comparison with maternal titers, examination, and treatment decisions guided by the evaluation. Maternal treatment alone does not clear fetal infection in that window, and a normal examination does not exclude infection in the neonate.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has chronic pelvic pain and severe dysmenorrhea that has not improved on NSAIDs and continuous combined pills. She wishes to avoid surgery for now. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start a GnRH antagonist or norethindrone acetate
Perform hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
Prescribe long-term opioid analgesia
Repeat the same pills at a higher estrogen dose
items.explanation: Empiric medical therapy for suspected endometriosis can proceed without laparoscopy, and when first-line treatment fails, options include progestins such as norethindrone acetate, GnRH agonists or antagonists with add-back therapy, and others. Hysterectomy is excessive in a young woman and does not guarantee relief. Chronic opioids are discouraged, and higher estrogen does not suppress the disease.

items.stem: Women in a randomized trial of a preventive drug are analyzed in the group to which they were assigned, even though some stopped taking the drug early. Which analytic approach does this describe?
options: Per-protocol analysis
Intention to treat
As-treated analysis
Noninferiority analysis
items.explanation: Analysis by intention to treat keeps every participant in the group to which she was randomized, regardless of adherence, which preserves the benefit of randomization. Per-protocol and as-treated analyses remove or regroup participants who did not follow the plan, which reintroduces the confounding that randomization had balanced. A noninferiority analysis asks whether a new treatment is not worse than the standard by a set margin, which is a different question.

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman reports chest pressure with exertion that radiates to the jaw, along with nausea and fatigue. She has hypertension and diabetes. Her resting electrocardiogram is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassurance because the electrocardiogram is normal
Treatment for anxiety with a benzodiazepine
Repeat evaluation only if pain occurs at rest
Stress testing with imaging
items.explanation: Women with exertional chest pressure and risk factors have a meaningful chance of coronary disease even when symptoms are atypical, and a normal resting electrocardiogram does not exclude it. Stress testing with imaging is the appropriate evaluation. Attributing symptoms to anxiety is a recognized source of missed diagnoses, and waiting for rest pain delays care.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman with a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion has a loop electrosurgical excision procedure. Pathology reports high-grade dysplasia at the endocervical margin. She is not pregnant and desires future fertility. What is the best next step?
options: Repeat excision or endocervical sampling
Immediate hysterectomy
Routine screening in three years
Annual cytology only, with no further sampling
items.explanation: Positive endocervical margins after excision for high-grade disease leave a higher risk of residual lesion, so repeat conization or sampling of the canal with close colposcopic follow-up is advised in a woman who wishes to preserve fertility. Hysterectomy is excessive without cancer, and routine screening or annual cytology alone is inadequate for this level of risk.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is varicella nonimmune on prenatal screening has just delivered a healthy term infant and is breastfeeding. She is ready for discharge. What is the best management of her varicella susceptibility?
options: Withhold the vaccine until she stops breastfeeding
Give varicella zoster immune globulin to her now
Give varicella vaccine before discharge, with a second dose later
Plan vaccination only if she is exposed in a future pregnancy
items.explanation: The live varicella vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy, so nonimmune women are vaccinated in the postpartum period, ideally before discharge, with a second dose four to eight weeks later. It is safe with breastfeeding. Immune globulin is for exposure, not routine prevention. Waiting until a later pregnancy forfeits the safe window, and deferring until weaning has no basis.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has 8 months of burning vulvar pain at the vaginal introitus with intercourse and tampon use. Examination shows normal skin, a negative wet mount, and a positive cotton swab test at 5 and 7 o'clock. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Lichen sclerosus
Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis
Herpes simplex infection
Provoked localized vulvodynia
items.explanation: Burning pain at the vestibule elicited by touch, with normal skin and negative microscopy, characterizes provoked vestibulodynia, a form of vulvodynia. Lichen sclerosus would produce white, thin, scarred skin with itching. Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis would show hyphae or a positive culture, and herpes would present with vesicles or ulcers and not with isolated touch-evoked pain. Treatment often combines pelvic floor therapy and topical agents.

items.stem: A woman with a pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variant that affects only some of her mitochondria asks about the risk to her future children. Her partner has no known genetic disease. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Half of her sons and half of her daughters will inherit the variant
All of her children can inherit the variant, with severity that varies by the proportion of affected mitochondria
Only her daughters will inherit the variant, because it is X-linked
Her children will be carriers only if her partner is also a carrier
items.explanation: Mitochondria are transmitted through the oocyte cytoplasm, so a mother can pass the variant to every child, while a father does not transmit it. Heteroplasmy, the mix of normal and variant genomes, explains why the proportion inherited and the clinical severity vary between siblings. Mendelian ratios do not apply, the pattern is not X-linked, and the partner's genotype is irrelevant to transmission.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman's mother and sister both carry a pathogenic MLH1 variant found on germline testing after the sister's colon cancer. She has no personal history of cancer and has not been tested. What is the best next step?
options: Order tumor immunohistochemistry on a blood sample
Defer all testing until she develops a cancer
Start colonoscopy at age 50 and skip genetic testing
Offer testing for the specific familial variant
items.explanation: When a pathogenic variant is known in the family, relatives are offered targeted testing for that exact variant, which is simpler and more informative than searching for an unknown one. A negative result returns her to average risk, while a positive result starts early colonoscopy and gynecologic counseling. Tumor staining needs tumor tissue, waiting for cancer defeats prevention, and average-risk screening ages are unsafe for a carrier.

items.stem: A 45-year-old with symptomatic fibroids and a 280 g uterus requires hysterectomy. She has no prolapse or prior abdominal surgery. Which approach is preferred when feasible?
options: Abdominal hysterectomy through a midline incision
Robotic-assisted supracervical hysterectomy only
Vaginal hysterectomy
Laparoscopic hysterectomy with uncontained morcellation
items.explanation: ACOG advises vaginal hysterectomy first when feasible, with laparoscopic hysterectomy as the next choice, because of lower morbidity, shorter recovery, and lower cost. Abdominal hysterectomy is reserved for cases in which minimally invasive routes are not possible. Supracervical hysterectomy is chosen by indication, not as a rule, and uncontained morcellation risks disseminating occult malignancy. Vaginal surgery avoids abdominal incisions altogether, which is why it leads the hierarchy of routes.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 at 14 weeks has an opioid use disorder and has taken buprenorphine for two years with stable function. She asks to stop it because of concern for the baby. What is the best recommendation?
options: Taper off the medication over two weeks
Continue buprenorphine in coordinated care
Switch to an as-needed short-acting opioid
Stop all medication and use only counseling
items.explanation: Medication for opioid use disorder with buprenorphine or methadone is the standard of care in pregnancy because it lowers relapse, overdose, and fetal exposure to illicit drugs. Rapid taper and abrupt cessation risk relapse and fetal stress. Short-acting opioids cause withdrawal swings, and counseling alone has a poor success rate. Neonatal opioid withdrawal is expected and treatable, not a reason to stop.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has sudden right lower quadrant pain with vomiting. Ultrasonography shows a 7 cm right ovary with a cystic mass and reduced venous flow, but arterial flow is still present. Which is the best management?
options: Urgent laparoscopy to detorse the ovary and preserve it
Right oophorectomy as the initial operation
Observation until Doppler flow is absent
Oral analgesics and repeat pelvic ultrasonography in three days
items.explanation: Ovarian torsion is a clinical diagnosis and preserved arterial flow does not exclude it. Prompt laparoscopic detorsion usually restores function even when the ovary looks dusky, so conservation is preferred in a young woman. Oophorectomy is unnecessarily radical. Waiting for flow to disappear risks infarction, and delayed reassessment prolongs ischemia. Torsion is a surgical diagnosis, and imaging cannot rule it out.

items.stem: A laboratory lowers the cutoff value that defines a positive result on a screening test for a gynecologic condition. Which change in test performance is expected?
options: Sensitivity decreases and specificity increases
Both sensitivity and specificity increase
Sensitivity increases and specificity decreases
Both sensitivity and specificity decrease
items.explanation: Lowering the threshold for positivity captures more truly affected people, so sensitivity rises and false negatives fall. The same change labels more unaffected people as positive, so specificity falls and false positives rise. Sensitivity and specificity move in opposite directions along a given test's curve, so both rising or both falling is not expected from changing the cutoff alone.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman asks for an HIV preexposure prophylaxis prescription because her partner has HIV with a detectable viral load. Her HIV test today is negative and her creatinine is normal. Which regimen is appropriate?
options: A single dose taken only after each exposure
Daily tenofovir with emtricitabine and testing every 3 months
Monotherapy with zidovudine for 28 days
No medication because condoms alone are required
items.explanation: Tenofovir with emtricitabine taken daily is the standard preexposure prophylaxis, with HIV, renal function, and sexually transmitted infection testing every 3 months. A post-exposure-only course is for nonoccupational exposure, not ongoing risk. Zidovudine monotherapy is not an accepted regimen, and condoms are advised in addition, not as the sole option. Adherence and creatinine are reviewed at each visit.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman needs abdominal hysterectomy for grade 2 endometrial cancer. She had a coronary stent placed 4 months ago and takes dual antiplatelet therapy. What is the most appropriate preoperative approach?
options: Stop both antiplatelet drugs 7 days before surgery
Replace both antiplatelet drugs with prophylactic anticoagulation
Postpone the cancer surgery until 12 months after the stent
Consult cardiology and continue aspirin through the operation
items.explanation: A stent placed within months carries a high risk of stent thrombosis when antiplatelet therapy stops, so aspirin is generally continued through surgery and the plan is coordinated with cardiology. Cancer surgery is time-sensitive, so it is not deferred for a full year without a reason. Stopping both drugs invites thrombosis, and substituting anticoagulation does not protect a stent. The balance between bleeding and thrombosis is individualized.

items.stem: A 34-year-old G3P2 at 18 weeks has fever, flank pain, and costovertebral tenderness. Her temperature is 39.2 degrees Celsius and a urine culture is pending. Which is the best initial management?
options: Admission with intravenous ceftriaxone
Outpatient nitrofurantoin for 7 days
A single oral dose of fosfomycin
Observation at home with oral hydration
items.explanation: Acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy is treated with admission, hydration, and intravenous antibiotics, since it can progress to sepsis and respiratory distress. Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin reach poor renal tissue concentrations and treat only lower tract infection. Simply observing delays treatment of a serious infection. After recovery, suppressive therapy is often given for the remainder of the pregnancy.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with syncope and lower abdominal pain. Her pulse is 128, blood pressure is 82/50, and her pregnancy test is positive. Focused ultrasonography shows free fluid in the pelvis and Morison pouch. What is the next step?
options: Methotrexate 50 mg per square meter intramuscularly
Serial hCG measurement in 48 hours
Surgery after resuscitation
Dilation and curettage in the office
items.explanation: A hemodynamically unstable patient with a positive pregnancy test and hemoperitoneum has a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise and needs immediate surgery with volume resuscitation. Methotrexate is only for stable patients without rupture. Waiting for repeat hCG delays lifesaving care, and curettage does not control intraperitoneal bleeding. Blood products should be available while the operating room is prepared.

items.stem: A 19-year-old with primary amenorrhea has normal breast development and scant pubic hair. Examination shows a blind-ending vagina, and testosterone is in the male range with a 46,XY karyotype. Which mechanism explains this presentation?
options: A defective androgen receptor that prevents virilization despite high testosterone
Deficient 5-alpha reductase that blocks conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone
Absent anti-mullerian hormone production by immature Sertoli cells
An SRY gene translocation onto the X chromosome
items.explanation: Complete androgen insensitivity results from a mutation in the X-linked androgen receptor; testosterone aromatizes to estradiol, giving breast development, while the lack of androgen action leaves scant body hair and a short vagina. Anti-mullerian hormone is made normally, so a uterus is absent. 5-alpha reductase deficiency virilizes at puberty. An SRY translocation produces 46,XX males.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman has no prior fractures, no family history of osteoporosis, and does not smoke. She has never had bone density testing. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: No screening until she has a fracture
Vitamin D level measurement alone
Screening with heel ultrasonography every year
Screening with dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry now
items.explanation: Guidelines recommend bone density screening for all women at age 65, using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry of the hip and spine, and earlier for younger postmenopausal women with risk factors. Waiting for a fracture misses the opportunity to prevent it. A vitamin D level does not measure bone density, and annual heel ultrasonography is not the standard diagnostic screening method.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman scheduled for abdominal hysterectomy has a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin. Which antibiotic prophylaxis is most appropriate?
options: Cefazolin alone before incision
Clindamycin plus gentamicin before incision
Ampicillin plus sulbactam before incision
Metronidazole alone before incision
items.explanation: For hysterectomy, cefazolin is the standard, but with a history of immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin, a cephalosporin is avoided. Recommended alternatives cover anaerobes and gram-negative organisms, such as clindamycin plus an aminoglycoside, or metronidazole plus an aminoglycoside. Ampicillin plus sulbactam is a penicillin, and metronidazole alone lacks adequate gram-negative coverage, so it is not enough as prophylaxis.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 at 39 weeks is in active labor on an oxytocin infusion. The tracing shows recurrent late decelerations with minimal variability and six contractions in 10 minutes. Which is the first action?
options: Stop the oxytocin and reposition the patient
Increase the oxytocin to strengthen contractions
Perform immediate cesarean delivery without other measures
Place a fetal scalp electrode and continue the infusion
items.explanation: Tachysystole with recurrent late decelerations indicates reduced uteroplacental perfusion, and the first step of intrauterine resuscitation is to stop or reduce oxytocin and change maternal position, with oxygen or fluid bolus as needed. Raising oxytocin worsens the problem. Cesarean is considered if the tracing fails to improve, and a scalp electrode adds monitoring but does not treat the cause.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with endometrial cancer has immunohistochemistry showing loss of MSH2 and MSH6 expression. Her sister had colon cancer at age 40. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure her that this is a sporadic cancer
Test only for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations
Refer for germline testing for Lynch
Offer testing only to her male relatives
items.explanation: Mismatch repair deficiency with a strong family history suggests Lynch syndrome, confirmed by germline testing for mismatch repair genes. Loss of MSH2 and MSH6 is not reassuring. BRCA testing addresses a different syndrome, and relatives of both sexes are offered testing once a pathogenic variant is found in the patient. Results also guide surveillance for colorectal and other cancers.

items.stem: A 21-year-old has urethral discharge and a positive nucleic acid amplification test for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Chlamydia testing is pending. Which is the preferred treatment?
options: Azithromycin 2 g orally once
Cefixime 400 mg orally once
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally once
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once
items.explanation: Because of widespread resistance, ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly is the recommended single-dose therapy for uncomplicated gonorrhea, and doxycycline for 7 days covers chlamydia when it is not excluded. Azithromycin monotherapy invites resistance. Oral cefixime is an alternative only when ceftriaxone is unavailable. Fluoroquinolones are no longer recommended because resistance is high. Recent partners should be treated, and the patient should abstain until both complete therapy.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman on postoperative day 5 after an abdominal hysterectomy with adhesiolysis has colicky abdominal pain and bilious vomiting. She is passing no flatus, bowel sounds are high-pitched, and radiographs show dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels and a collapsed colon. What is the initial management?
options: Immediate discharge on a clear liquid diet
Nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluids, and serial abdominal examinations
Neostigmine infusion
Prokinetic therapy with early solid feeding
items.explanation: Colicky pain, bilious vomiting, and dilated small bowel with a collapsed colon indicate mechanical small bowel obstruction from adhesions, unlike ileus where bowel sounds are absent and gas is diffuse. Initial care is bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, fluid and electrolyte replacement, and serial examinations, with surgery for peritonitis or failure. Feeding, prokinetics, or neostigmine are for ileus and can worsen obstruction.

items.stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks in labor has a category II tracing with minimal variability and no accelerations. The baseline is 150 bpm and recurrent variable decelerations occur. Which maneuver best helps assess fetal acid-base status?
options: Maternal oral hydration and observation for one hour
Cord blood gas collection before delivery
Repeated vaginal examinations every 5 minutes
Fetal scalp stimulation looking for an acceleration
items.explanation: In a category II tracing with minimal variability, an acceleration after scalp stimulation or vibroacoustic stimulation reliably suggests that the fetal pH is above 7.20 and reassures the team. Oral hydration does not assess status. A cord gas can only be drawn after birth, and frequent vaginal examinations add infection risk without giving information about oxygenation.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with a body mass index of 38 has postmenopausal bleeding. Endometrial biopsy shows endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia without cancer on pathology review. Imaging shows no mass. She has completed childbearing. What is the preferred treatment?
options: Observation with repeat biopsy in a year
Oral estrogen therapy to stabilize the lining
Total hysterectomy
Endometrial ablation
items.explanation: Endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia carries a substantial risk of coexisting or later carcinoma, and hysterectomy is the standard treatment for women who have finished childbearing. Observation or estrogen would allow progression. Ablation destroys part of the lining and prevents later sampling of residual tissue, which could hide an advancing cancer. Progestin therapy is reserved for those who wish to preserve fertility.

items.stem: A 32-year-old at a routine visit reports that her partner threatens her and controls her money, and she has bruises on her upper arms. She says she is afraid to go home. What is the best next step?
options: Validate her, assess safety, and offer advocacy referral and a safety plan
Report to law enforcement without her consent, as is required in every case
Recommend couples counseling with her partner
Document the bruising and schedule a follow-up visit in 6 months
items.explanation: A nonjudgmental response, safety assessment, and offering advocacy and a safety plan support the patient's autonomy. Mandatory reporting laws for adult intimate partner violence vary and generally do not apply without consent. Couples counseling can escalate danger. Delaying follow-up by months leaves an at-risk woman without help when she has stated she is afraid. Chart review should record her words, injuries, and referrals in a manner that she controls.

items.stem: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman has a firm, painless 3 cm mass in the left Bartholin gland region that has enlarged over 2 months. There is no fever or erythema. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Incision and drainage with a Word catheter alone
Excisional biopsy of the mass to exclude carcinoma
Oral antibiotics for 10 days and reassessment
Warm sitz baths and reassurance
items.explanation: A new Bartholin gland mass in a woman aged 40 or older raises concern for Bartholin gland carcinoma, so tissue is needed rather than simple drainage. Excisional biopsy provides the pathology. A Word catheter treats a benign abscess or cyst and would leave a malignancy undiagnosed. Antibiotics do not treat a solid painless mass without infection, and reassurance with sitz baths delays diagnosis in this age group.

items.stem: A 24-year-old G1P1 has just delivered and the clinician sees a large mass at the introitus, with bleeding and the placenta still attached. The fundus cannot be palpated abdominally. What should be done first?
options: Pull on the cord to deliver the placenta first
Give additional uterotonics until bleeding slows
Wait for spontaneous reduction over several hours
Stop oxytocin and replace the uterus now
items.explanation: Uterine inversion is an emergency, and the uterus should be replaced immediately by pushing the fundus up through the cervix, with uterotonics stopped and a relaxant such as terbutaline or nitroglycerin given if needed. Traction on the cord or removing the placenta first increases hemorrhage. Further uterotonics tighten the ring, and delay risks shock from vagal reaction and bleeding.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman finds a 2 cm mobile, smooth, rubbery breast mass. It does not change with her cycle. Ultrasonography shows a well-circumscribed oval hypoechoic mass wider than tall. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Core biopsy or imaging follow up by shared decision
Immediate mastectomy
Screening mammography only
Reassure her and discharge without follow-up
items.explanation: In women younger than 30, ultrasound is the preferred imaging test, and a probable fibroadenoma may be confirmed by core biopsy or followed with serial imaging after shared decision making. Mastectomy is far too aggressive. Mammography is less useful in dense young breasts, and discharge without any plan is inappropriate for a new solid mass.

items.stem: A 15-year-old comes to the clinic with her mother and requests contraception. Her mother is in the room. What is the best approach to the visit?
options: Ask her mother to answer the sexual history questions
Defer the sexual history until she turns 18
Interview her alone and explain the limits of confidentiality
Require parental consent before discussing contraception
items.explanation: Adolescents are entitled to private time; explaining confidentiality and its limits (such as risk of harm or abuse) improves honest disclosure and care. Having a parent answer defeats the purpose. Delaying the history withholds needed counseling. Many jurisdictions allow minors to consent to contraception, and requiring parental consent can deter care. Her confidential visit should still include screening for infection, safety, and vaccines.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G3P2 at 37 weeks has spontaneous rupture of membranes with a breech presentation. The cervix is 4 cm and a pulsating loop of cord is palpated. Fetal bradycardia follows. Which is the best immediate action?
options: Attempt to replace the cord into the vagina
Elevate the presenting part and proceed to cesarean
Start oxytocin to accelerate delivery
Place her supine and observe the tracing for 20 minutes
items.explanation: Cord prolapse needs immediate relief of cord compression: the examiner's hand elevates the presenting part until delivery, and the patient is positioned knee to chest or Trendelenburg while an emergency cesarean is arranged. Replacing the cord is ineffective and dangerous. Oxytocin does not speed delivery enough to matter, and observing allows continued compression and hypoxic injury.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman notices blood-tinged fluid leaking without squeezing from one duct of the left nipple. Examination reveals no mass, and her mammogram is normal. Which is the best next step?
options: Diagnostic ultrasonography and possible duct excision
Reassurance and routine screening in a year
Start oral antibiotics for presumed lactational mastitis
Measure serum prolactin only
items.explanation: Unilateral, spontaneous, single-duct bloody discharge is suspicious for an intraductal papilloma or, less often, cancer, and warrants diagnostic imaging and possible excision. Reassurance risks missing a lesion. Mastitis is painful with erythema, and prolactin evaluates bilateral, milky, multiduct discharge, which is a different presentation. Excision also provides tissue to exclude papillary carcinoma, and imaging helps localize the lesion before surgery. Cytology of discharge is unreliable.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has never received the recombinant zoster vaccine and has no immune-compromising condition. Which immunization schedule is recommended?
options: A single dose, with a booster every 10 years
Two doses given 2 to 6 months apart
Two doses given 2 weeks apart
Not recommended at her age
items.explanation: Recombinant zoster vaccine is a two-dose series offered from age 50, with the doses given 2 to 6 months apart. A single dose with a ten-year booster describes tetanus-containing vaccines, not this product. An interval of 2 weeks is too short to complete the series as intended. Waiting until an older age is unnecessary because eligibility begins at 50, so she should start the series now.

items.stem: A 35-year-old G4P3 develops sudden dyspnea, hypotension, and cyanosis soon after a vaginal delivery, followed by seizure and then profuse bleeding with prolonged coagulation times. Which diagnosis best explains this sequence?
options: Massive pulmonary thromboembolism with shock
Uterine atony with vasovagal collapse
Amniotic fluid embolism
Eclampsia complicated by retained placenta
items.explanation: Amniotic fluid embolism classically presents with abrupt cardiorespiratory collapse around delivery, often with seizures and then disseminated intravascular coagulation causing hemorrhage. Management is supportive: oxygenation, vasopressors, and blood products. Pulmonary embolism seldom produces profound coagulopathy. Atony causes bleeding without the cardiopulmonary collapse and coagulation failure, and eclampsia would show severe hypertension first. Early recognition prompts activation of the massive transfusion protocol.

items.stem: A 27-year-old G1P1 had a vaginal delivery with a midline extension. The sphincter repair after delivery was described as involving more than 50 percent of the external anal sphincter thickness with an intact internal sphincter. How is this injury classified?
options: Second-degree laceration
Third-degree 3a laceration
Fourth-degree laceration with mucosal tear
Third-degree 3b laceration
items.explanation: A third-degree laceration involves the anal sphincter complex, subclassified as 3a when less than 50 percent of the external sphincter is torn, 3b when more than 50 percent is torn, and 3c when the internal sphincter is also torn. A second-degree injury spares the sphincter, and a fourth-degree tear extends through the anal mucosa. Accurate grading matters because it dictates repair technique and antibiotic prophylaxis.

items.stem: A healthy 41-year-old woman with no family history of cancer and no breast symptoms asks when she should start screening mammography. What is the best response?
options: Wait until age 50 and then screen every 5 years
Order annual breast magnetic resonance imaging
Begin screening mammography now, and repeat it at least every 2 years
Rely on clinical breast examination alone until age 55
items.explanation: For women at average risk, screening mammography is recommended every 2 years from age 40 through 74, and some organizations accept annual screening with shared decision making about the start. Waiting until 50 reflects older guidance, and a 5-year interval is too long. Magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for women at high risk, such as a lifetime risk of 20 percent or more. Clinical examination alone misses early cancers.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 at 33 weeks has a known complete placenta previa and has had no bleeding. She asks about the timing of delivery. Which is the most appropriate plan?
options: Induction of labor at 39 weeks
Scheduled cesarean at 34 weeks regardless of bleeding
Expectant management until spontaneous labor
Cesarean delivery between 36 0/7 and 37 6/7 weeks
items.explanation: For uncomplicated placenta previa, cesarean delivery is planned from 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks, which balances the risk of bleeding against neonatal prematurity. Induction and labor with a complete previa are unsafe. Delivery at 34 weeks is reserved for bleeding patients or those with suspected accreta, and waiting for labor risks hemorrhage when the cervix begins to change.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman has constant vaginal leakage after a hysterectomy. A vaginal tampon is not stained after methylene blue is instilled in the bladder, and renal ultrasonography shows left hydronephrosis. Which study best confirms the site of the fistula?
options: CT urography with delayed images
Voiding cystourethrography
Repeat cystoscopy with dye in the bladder
Transabdominal pelvic ultrasonography
items.explanation: Negative retrograde dye staining with hydronephrosis suggests a ureteral injury and fistula. CT urography with delayed excretory images shows ureteral anatomy, extravasation, and the fistula site. Voiding cystourethrography shows bladder and urethral leaks but not the ureter, repeating bladder dye staining adds nothing, and ultrasound can only show hydronephrosis without ever identifying the exact site.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a 25 pack-year smoking history and quit 5 years ago. She has no symptoms. Which screening is recommended?
options: Annual chest radiograph with sputum review
Annual low-dose chest computed tomography
Sputum cytology every 6 months
No screening, because she has quit smoking
items.explanation: Adults aged 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years should have annual low-dose computed tomography. Chest radiography and sputum cytology do not reduce lung cancer mortality. Having quit 5 years ago does not exempt her, since she remains within the 15-year window. Screening stops once she has been a nonsmoker for 15 years or develops limiting health problems.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 has persistent bleeding two hours after delivery with a soft, boggy uterus despite fundal massage and oxytocin. She has asthma and normal blood pressure. Which second-line uterotonic is the best choice?
options: Methylergonovine 0.2 mg intramuscularly
Carboprost tromethamine 0.25 mg intramuscularly
Terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously
Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously
items.explanation: Methylergonovine is effective for atony and is acceptable when blood pressure is normal, making it suitable for this asthmatic patient. Carboprost can trigger bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma. Terbutaline and magnesium sulfate relax the uterus and would worsen atony, since both are tocolytic agents used for other purposes such as inversion or neuroprotection. Bleeding unresponsive to this drug needs escalation to surgical measures.

items.stem: An adolescent brought to clinic by her mother has no menses at age 13 and months of recurring lower abdominal pain. Breast development is normal. Examination shows a bulging bluish membrane at the introitus and a lower abdominal mass. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Combined oral contraceptives to induce menses
Observation until menarche occurs spontaneously
Vaginal dilator therapy for several months
Surgical hymenotomy to drain the hematocolpos
items.explanation: This presentation indicates an imperforate hymen with obstructed menstrual blood, now causing hematocolpos, and the definitive treatment is a hymenotomy to release it. Hormones suppress menses but leave the obstruction in place. Observation allows progression of pain and the risk of retrograde flow and endometriosis, and dilators are used for vaginal agenesis, not for a membrane.

items.stem: A 36-year-old G3P2 at 34 weeks reports painless vaginal bleeding after spontaneous rupture of membranes. The fetal heart rate becomes sinusoidal and the bleeding is dark red. Ultrasonography earlier showed a velamentous cord insertion crossing the cervix. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Placental abruption with concealed bleeding
Uterine rupture at a prior cesarean scar
Vasa previa with ruptured fetal vessels
Cervical polyp with minor contact bleeding
items.explanation: Fetal vessels crossing the cervix are unprotected by cord or placenta and tear when membranes rupture, causing fetal exsanguination, often with a sinusoidal tracing. Immediate cesarean is needed. Abruption is painful and usually associated with a tense uterus, and uterine rupture presents with pain and loss of station. A polyp bleeds from maternal tissue and does not cause fetal heart rate changes.

items.stem: A 16-year-old has never menstruated. She is 144 cm tall with a webbed neck, no breast development, and an FSH of 78 mIU/mL. Which study establishes the diagnosis?
options: Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging
Peripheral blood karyotype
Serum prolactin and thyroid-stimulating hormone
Progestin withdrawal challenge
items.explanation: Short stature, a webbed neck, absent puberty, and high FSH indicate hypergonadotropic hypogonadism from gonadal dysgenesis, most often 45,X Turner syndrome, confirmed by karyotype. Imaging may show a small uterus but does not give the cause. Prolactin and thyroid tests evaluate hypogonadotropic or euthyroid causes. A progestin challenge is pointless when estrogen is absent and the ovaries have failed.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 at 7 weeks has hCG 180,000 mIU/mL and an ultrasound showing a heterogeneous echogenic uterine mass with many small cystic spaces and no fetus. Chest radiograph is normal. What is the best management?
options: Methotrexate with serial hCG until negative
Observation until spontaneous passage of the mass
Hysterectomy with immediate adjuvant chemotherapy
Suction curettage, then weekly hCG measurements
items.explanation: A complete hydatidiform mole is treated by suction evacuation, followed by weekly hCG measurements until three consecutive undetectable results, then monthly surveillance. Methotrexate is for persistent or ectopic disease, not for initial evacuation. Expectant management risks bleeding and persistent disease, and hysterectomy is an option only for women who have completed childbearing, without requiring chemotherapy at first.

items.stem: A 26-year-old has oligomenorrhea, facial hirsutism, and polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasound. Which laboratory evaluation is required before diagnosing polycystic ovary syndrome?
options: Anti-mullerian hormone and inhibin B on cycle day 3
Fasting insulin and C-peptide only
Thyroid-stimulating hormone, prolactin, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate and cortisol-binding globulin
items.explanation: Polycystic ovary syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion; thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, and nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (screened by morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone) mimic it and must be excluded. Anti-mullerian hormone is not a diagnostic requirement, insulin testing does not exclude mimics, and cortisol-binding globulin is irrelevant, though adrenal androgens are checked when virilization is rapid. Elevated androgens from a tumor would instead show rapid virilization and a very high testosterone.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 with a prior cesarean has spotting at 8 weeks. Ultrasonography shows an empty cavity and a gestational sac in the cornual region of the uterus, surrounded by less than 5 mm of myometrium, with a visible interstitial line. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Interstitial ectopic pregnancy
Cervical pregnancy
Intrauterine pregnancy in a bicornuate uterus
Cesarean scar pregnancy
items.explanation: A sac eccentrically placed in the cornual region with a thin surrounding myometrial mantle and an interstitial line sign defines an interstitial (cornual) ectopic pregnancy. It carries a high risk of rupture and hemorrhage. A cervical pregnancy lies in the cervical canal, a scar pregnancy sits in the anterior lower segment at the incision, and a bicornuate uterus pregnancy would show a normal thick myometrium.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman with a body mass index of 38 has had irregular, heavy bleeding for 8 months. Pregnancy test is negative and hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL. What is the best next step?
options: Start a combined oral contraceptive and reassess in 6 months
Endometrial biopsy
Order a hysterosalpingogram
Schedule endometrial ablation
items.explanation: Chronic anovulation with obesity gives unopposed estrogen exposure, so endometrial sampling is indicated even below age 45 when risk factors or persistent bleeding exist. Hormonal treatment before excluding hyperplasia or cancer is premature. Hysterosalpingography examines tubes, not the lining. Ablation should follow a benign biopsy result, since it can hide later malignancy. Atypical or malignant disease is found in a meaningful minority of such patients, so waiting is unsafe.

items.stem: A 24-year-old G1P0 at 10 weeks has had persistent vomiting for 2 weeks, with 8 percent weight loss and ketonuria. Which should be given before intravenous dextrose to prevent a neurologic complication?
options: Thiamine
Pyridoxine
Ondansetron
Folic acid
items.explanation: Prolonged vomiting depletes thiamine, and giving dextrose before replacing it can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy, so thiamine should be given first in hyperemesis gravidarum. Pyridoxine and ondansetron help symptoms but do not protect against this complication, and folic acid is taken for neural tube prevention. Intravenous fluids and electrolyte correction follow thiamine. Antiemetics and correction of ketosis are given alongside it.

items.stem: A 28-year-old at an estimated 6 weeks has a hemoglobin of 12.8 g/dL, stable vital signs, a 2.2 cm unruptured adnexal mass, and an hCG of 3,200 mIU/mL. Which finding would contraindicate methotrexate?
options: An hCG level above 1,500 mIU/mL
Elevated creatinine and transaminases showing organ dysfunction
A mass size under 3.5 cm
A prior ectopic pregnancy treated with salpingectomy
items.explanation: Methotrexate is renally cleared and hepatotoxic, so impaired kidney or liver function, along with breastfeeding, immunodeficiency, and hemodynamic instability, is a contraindication. An hCG over 5,000 and fetal cardiac activity lower success but an hCG of 3,200 is acceptable. A mass under 3.5 cm favors success, and a prior ectopic is not a contraindication. Free fluid with pain or instability would instead call for surgery rather than medical therapy.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman is certain of her last menstrual period, which gives 10 weeks 3 days. First-trimester ultrasound shows a crown-rump length consistent with 9 weeks 2 days. How should the due date be assigned?
options: Keep the menstrual dating, because a certain period outranks crown-rump length
Keep the menstrual dating and repeat the scan in 2 weeks to confirm growth
Redate by ultrasound, since the difference exceeds 7 days at this age
Redate only if the difference exceeds 10 days at this gestational age
items.explanation: Between 9 0/7 and 13 6/7 weeks, a discrepancy greater than 7 days between menstrual and crown-rump dating calls for ultrasound redating; the threshold is 5 days before 9 0/7 weeks. Here the gap is 8 days. Certainty of the period does not override the rule, a repeat scan adds nothing, and the 10-day threshold applies only later, at 16 to 21 weeks.

items.stem: A 42-year-old has heavy menstrual bleeding and a pelvic pressure sensation. Examination shows a 14-week-size, irregular uterus. She wants to keep her uterus and is not trying to conceive. Which option offers fibroid treatment without surgery?
options: Dilation and curettage with hysteroscopy
Clomiphene citrate
Etonogestrel implant placement
Uterine artery embolization
items.explanation: Uterine artery embolization shrinks leiomyomas by occluding their blood supply and preserves the uterus, which suits a woman who declines hysterectomy and does not desire pregnancy. Dilation and curettage does not treat intramural fibroids. Clomiphene induces ovulation and would not control bleeding. A progestin implant may cause irregular bleeding and does not reduce fibroid size.

items.stem: An Rh(D)-negative woman delivers an Rh(D)-positive infant. A rosette test is positive, and a Kleihauer-Betke test estimates a fetomaternal hemorrhage of about 45 mL of fetal whole blood. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Give a single standard 300 mcg dose only
Withhold Rh immune globulin because sensitization has already occurred
Give additional Rh immune globulin doses based on the calculated volume
Repeat the antibody screen in 6 months before any treatment
items.explanation: One standard 300 mcg dose covers about 30 mL of fetal whole blood. When quantification shows a larger fetomaternal hemorrhage, the calculated number of vials, with an added vial, is given to prevent alloimmunization. A single dose is inadequate here, and sensitization is not established until antibodies develop, so treatment is still effective. Delaying by months forfeits the protective window.

items.stem: A 29-year-old has severe dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, and painful defecation during menses. Pelvic examination shows uterosacral nodularity. Transvaginal ultrasound is unremarkable. What is the best next step?
options: Perform diagnostic laparoscopy before any medical therapy
Empiric hormonal suppression
Begin a 3-month course of empiric antibiotics
Order serum CA-125 to confirm the diagnosis
items.explanation: A typical clinical picture of endometriosis justifies empiric treatment without surgical confirmation; hormonal suppression with NSAIDs relieves pain, and laparoscopy is held for treatment failure or an unclear diagnosis. Antibiotics treat pelvic infection, not this picture. CA-125 is elevated in many conditions, lacks adequate sensitivity and specificity, and is not recommended for diagnosis. Surgery is reserved for failed empiric therapy, a doubtful diagnosis, or a mass needing excision.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 32 weeks has a headache and blood pressure of 168/112 mm Hg, confirmed 15 minutes later. Urine protein is 3+. Which is the best next step?
options: Magnesium sulfate and prompt blood pressure treatment
Give oral methyldopa and reassess in 24 hours as an outpatient
Obtain a 24-hour urine collection before choosing any treatment
Give betamethasone and delay antihypertensive therapy until 34 weeks
items.explanation: Persistent systolic pressure of 160 or higher or diastolic of 110 or higher is a hypertensive emergency that needs treatment within 30 to 60 minutes with labetalol, hydralazine, or oral nifedipine, plus magnesium for seizure prophylaxis given the severe-range pressure and headache. Methyldopa is too slow, the diagnosis does not wait on a timed urine collection, and steroids do not replace blood pressure control.

items.stem: A 28-year-old has a routine screening cytology showing atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance. Reflex HPV testing is negative. What is the recommended management?
options: Colposcopy with biopsy now
Repeat cytology in 1 year
Loop electrosurgical excision procedure
Return for repeat screening in 3 years
items.explanation: ASC-US with negative high-risk HPV carries a very low risk of CIN 3 or worse, comparable to a negative cotest, so return in 3 years is advised. Colposcopy is for HPV-positive ASC-US. A 1-year repeat applies to certain HPV-positive results with low-grade findings in specific settings. Excision is for histologic high-grade disease and not a reasonable response to a negative HPV result.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 at 13 weeks has a nuchal translucency of 4.0 mm. Cell-free DNA screening for common aneuploidies is low risk. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Detailed anatomy ultrasound and fetal echocardiography
Routine care, since the cell-free DNA result is reassuring
Repeat the nuchal translucency measurement at 20 weeks
Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein only
items.explanation: A nuchal translucency of 3.0 mm or more is associated with structural defects, especially congenital heart disease, and genetic syndromes, even when common aneuploidy screening is normal. Targeted evaluation with detailed ultrasonography and fetal echocardiography is recommended, with diagnostic testing offered. Cell-free DNA does not exclude cardiac or other anomalies, and waiting or relying on alpha-fetoprotein misses them.

items.stem: A 38-year-old, with a confirmed pathogenic MSH2 variant and one child, completes childbearing. Which is the most effective cancer risk-reduction strategy?
options: Annual endometrial biopsy alone until age 60
Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
Bilateral salpingectomy with ovarian conservation
Continuous combined oral contraceptive use
items.explanation: Lynch syndrome carries a high lifetime risk of endometrial cancer that can exceed the colorectal risk, with an increased ovarian risk as well. Hysterectomy with oophorectomy, offered after childbearing, drastically reduces both. Biopsy alone is surveillance, not prevention, and cannot eliminate risk. Salpingectomy leaves the uterus and ovaries in place, and contraceptives lower risk only partially.

items.stem: A 31-year-old at 28 weeks has gestational diabetes well controlled on insulin with normal growth. At what gestational age is delivery recommended?
options: 37 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks
38 0/7 to 38 6/7 weeks
40 0/7 to 40 6/7 weeks
39 0/7 to 39 6/7 weeks
items.explanation: For medication-treated gestational diabetes with good control, delivery is advised between 39 0/7 and 39 6/7 weeks, balancing stillbirth risk against neonatal respiratory morbidity. Poor control or vascular disease moves delivery earlier, to 36 0/7 to 38 6/7 weeks. Diet-controlled disease can wait to 40 6/7 weeks. Intermediate windows apply to other risk categories rather than this one.

items.stem: A 33-year-old with 2 years of infertility has regular cycles. Her husband has a normal semen analysis. Hysterosalpingography shows bilateral hydrosalpinx with no spill. What should be recommended?
options: Intrauterine insemination with clomiphene for 6 cycles
Expectant management for another 12 months
In vitro fertilization, with consideration of salpingectomy beforehand
Tubal flushing with oil-based contrast alone
items.explanation: Bilateral tubal occlusion cannot be bypassed by insemination, and hydrosalpinx fluid reduces implantation, so IVF is indicated and salpingectomy before transfer improves outcomes. Insemination requires at least one patent tube. Waiting wastes time in a woman over 30 with a known mechanical barrier. Flushing is unlikely to open a hydrosalpinx and does not remove the harmful fluid.

items.stem: During delivery of a vertex fetus, the head has rotated internally and now crowns. Which cardinal movement occurs next?
options: Restitution
Extension
Flexion
External rotation
items.explanation: After engagement, descent, flexion, and internal rotation, the occiput passes beneath the pubic symphysis and the head extends to deliver the brow, face, and chin. Restitution and external rotation occur after the head delivers, as the shoulders rotate into the anteroposterior diameter. Flexion happens earlier, when the chin approaches the chest during descent. The full sequence is engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, and external rotation.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a 12 cm complex pelvic mass, ascites, an elevated CA-125, and a normal chest CT. Which finding on staging laparotomy would indicate the highest stage?
options: Involvement of both ovaries
Positive peritoneal washings only
Parenchymal liver metastasis
Pelvic extension to the uterus
items.explanation: Parenchymal liver metastases, along with distant spread, define stage IVB ovarian cancer. Bilateral ovarian disease is stage IB, positive washings alone raise stage IC, and pelvic extension to the uterus or tubes is stage IIA. Stage reflects the farthest spread, and distant organ involvement outranks local pelvic involvement regardless of tumor size. Distant organ involvement, rather than tumor size or bilaterality, drives the stage assignment.

items.stem: A 30-year-old at 40 weeks with one prior low transverse cesarean wishes to attempt labor. The cervix is closed, thick, and posterior. Which ripening method is preferred?
options: Vaginal misoprostol 25 mcg every 4 hours
Oral misoprostol 50 mcg every 4 hours
High-dose oxytocin infusion without ripening
Transcervical balloon catheter
items.explanation: Prostaglandin E1 (misoprostol) is avoided in women with a prior uterine scar because it increases uterine rupture risk. A balloon catheter ripens mechanically without raising rupture rates substantially. Oxytocin can be used once the cervix is favorable but is ineffective alone on a closed thick cervix, and high doses add rupture risk. Mechanical ripening is therefore the safest route toward vaginal birth after cesarean when the cervix is unfavorable.

items.stem: A 46-year-old reports leakage of urine with coughing and lifting but no urgency. Pelvic examination shows good support and a normal postvoid residual. Which is the appropriate initial treatment?
options: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training
Midurethral sling placement under local anesthesia
Anticholinergic medication
Intradetrusor botulinum toxin injection
items.explanation: Pelvic floor muscle training is first-line for stress urinary incontinence and may be combined with weight loss and a continence pessary. Slings are offered if conservative care fails. Anticholinergics treat urgency incontinence and would worsen retention. Botulinum toxin treats refractory overactive bladder and is not appropriate for stress incontinence in a woman without urgency. Weight loss of even a modest amount can further reduce leakage episodes.

items.stem: A 27-year-old multipara at 39 weeks is at 6 cm with ruptured membranes. The tracing shows recurrent variable decelerations to 70 bpm lasting 60 seconds, moderate variability, and a baseline of 140 bpm. Contractions occur every 3 minutes. What is the most appropriate initial response?
options: Proceed to immediate cesarean delivery for a category III tracing
Give terbutaline to stop all contractions
Begin oxytocin augmentation to shorten the labor
Reposition and consider amnioinfusion
items.explanation: Recurrent variable decelerations with moderate variability form a category II tracing and reflect cord compression, so the first steps are repositioning the mother and checking for rapid cervical progress. If the pattern persists, amnioinfusion of warmed saline can relieve compression, particularly with reduced fluid. Moderate variability is reassuring, so category III management and cesarean are not needed. Terbutaline treats tachysystole, and oxytocin would intensify cord compression.

items.stem: A 22-year-old has lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, and a temperature of 37.9 C. She is not pregnant and can tolerate oral medication. Which outpatient regimen is recommended?
options: Azithromycin 1 g orally once
Ceftriaxone once, then doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days
Doxycycline alone for 7 days
Ceftriaxone intramuscularly once with no further therapy
items.explanation: Mild to moderate pelvic inflammatory disease is treated with a single ceftriaxone dose plus 14 days of doxycycline and metronidazole, covering gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes. Single-dose azithromycin and a short doxycycline course are inadequate. Ceftriaxone alone leaves chlamydia and anaerobes untreated, raising the risk of persistent infection and tubal scarring. Partners from the previous 60 days should be tested and treated, and intercourse avoided until treatment ends.

items.stem: A 25-year-old nulligravid woman at 22 weeks has a transvaginal cervical length of 1.2 cm on a routine scan. She has no history of preterm birth. Which intervention is recommended?
options: Strict bed rest in the hospital
Immediate cervical cerclage
Vaginal progesterone daily until 36 weeks
Weekly intramuscular 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate
items.explanation: For a singleton pregnancy with no prior spontaneous preterm birth and a cervical length of 20 mm or less before 24 weeks, vaginal progesterone lowers the risk of early delivery. Cerclage is reserved for prior preterm birth with a short cervix, or for painless dilation. Bed rest is not effective, and the intramuscular formulation is intended for prior preterm birth and is no longer marketed.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman was treated for trichomoniasis two weeks ago with her partner treated at the same time. She is now asymptomatic and asks about follow-up. What is the recommended approach?
options: Retest in about 3 months, regardless of symptoms
No retesting unless symptoms recur
A test of cure today with wet mount only
Treat her partner again without testing her
items.explanation: Trichomonas vaginalis has high rates of reinfection and persistent infection, so women treated for it are advised to retest, ideally by nucleic acid amplification, about three months after treatment even if asymptomatic. Wet mount is insensitive and a test performed too soon may detect nonviable organisms. Waiting for symptoms misses asymptomatic reinfection, and retreating a partner without testing is not guideline care.

items.stem: A healthy 29-year-old G1P0 with an uncomplicated pregnancy and accurate dating reaches 41 weeks 0 days. Her cervix is closed and long, and fetal testing is reassuring. Which management is best supported?
options: Continue expectant care with no testing until she labors
Schedule cesarean delivery because the cervix is unfavorable
Delay induction until at least 43 weeks
Offer induction of labor, which is recommended by 42 0/7 weeks
items.explanation: Induction is offered from 41 0/7 to 41 6/7 weeks and is recommended no later than 42 0/7 weeks, because stillbirth, macrosomia, meconium aspiration, and oligohydramnios rise with each added week. A closed cervix calls for ripening, not cesarean. Waiting with no testing accepts avoidable risk, and delaying to 43 weeks exceeds every recommendation. If she declines induction, antenatal testing begins by 41 weeks.

items.stem: A 54-year-old, 3 years after her final menstrual period, has severe hot flashes and vaginal dryness. She has no contraindications and her uterus is intact. Which therapy is appropriate for her vasomotor symptoms?
options: Systemic estrogen without any progestogen opposition
Vaginal estrogen cream alone
Systemic estrogen with a progestogen
Progestin implant alone
items.explanation: Systemic estrogen is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms, and a progestogen is added in women with a uterus to prevent endometrial hyperplasia. Unopposed estrogen would raise cancer risk. Low-dose vaginal estrogen treats local dryness but does not reliably control hot flashes. A progestin implant alone has no meaningful effect on vasomotor symptoms. Genitourinary symptoms may be treated with added local estrogen if dryness persists despite systemic therapy.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman, 6 weeks after a vaginal delivery, is exclusively breastfeeding and wants contraception with no effect on milk supply. She has no medical problems. Which method is most appropriate?
options: Combined estrogen and progestin vaginal ring
Etonogestrel implant
Combined oral contraceptive pill
Transdermal estrogen patch
items.explanation: Progestin-only methods such as the implant, levonorgestrel intrauterine device, and depot medroxyprogesterone acetate do not impair lactation and are highly effective. Estrogen-containing methods may reduce milk volume, and in the early postpartum period they are also discouraged because of venous thromboembolism risk. The ring, pill, and patch all carry estrogen and are therefore less suitable here.

items.stem: A 68-year-old has a vaginal bulge and difficulty emptying her bladder. Examination shows the cervix and anterior vaginal wall descending 3 cm beyond the hymen. She wishes to avoid surgery. Which is the best initial option?
options: Vaginal pessary with fitting and follow-up
Abdominal sacrocolpopexy with synthetic mesh placement
Anterior colporrhaphy with mesh
Colpocleisis
items.explanation: A pessary is an effective, low-risk first-line treatment for symptomatic prolapse and suits a woman who declines surgery. Sacrocolpopexy and mesh repairs are operations she wishes to avoid. Colpocleisis is an obliterative surgery for women who are no longer sexually active and want definitive treatment, so it fits neither her preference nor a first step.

items.stem: A 24-year-old at 30 weeks reports a gush of clear fluid. Pooling is seen on speculum examination, nitrazine paper is positive, and fern testing is positive. She has no contractions. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Discharge home with pelvic rest and return precautions
Begin tocolysis with magnesium sulfate alone
Admit, give latency antibiotics and corticosteroids, and monitor closely
Induce labor now with oxytocin to avoid intraamniotic infection
items.explanation: Before 34 weeks, rupture of membranes without infection, labor, or fetal compromise is managed expectantly in hospital with latency antibiotics and antenatal corticosteroids, and delivery is planned at 34 0/7 weeks. Outpatient care is unsafe given infection risk, tocolysis offers no benefit once membranes have ruptured, and immediate induction at this gestational age forfeits steroid benefit.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 24 weeks had a thyroidectomy for Graves disease before pregnancy and now takes levothyroxine. Her thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin level is markedly elevated. What is the most appropriate fetal surveillance?
options: No additional surveillance, because she is euthyroid
Serial ultrasonography for fetal goiter and tachycardia
Amniocentesis for thyroid hormones in all cases
Administration of antithyroid drugs to the mother
items.explanation: Maternal thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin crosses the placenta and can cause fetal thyrotoxicosis even after ablation or surgery has made the mother hypothyroid. High titers, generally more than three times the upper limit, call for serial ultrasound looking for goiter, tachycardia, growth restriction, and hydrops. Maternal euthyroidism does not predict fetal status, and giving antithyroid drugs to a mother on replacement would cause fetal harm.

items.stem: A 24-year-old at 30 weeks with secondary syphilis receives intramuscular benzathine penicillin G. Eight hours later she has a temperature of 38.4 C, myalgias, and uterine contractions, and the tracing shows late decelerations. Which statement is correct?
options: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with supportive care
Penicillin anaphylaxis, so epinephrine and no further penicillin
